claims.text: Applying an ultra-thin, conformal Al2O3 coating by atomic layer deposition will significantly improve the oxidation resistance of a metallic substrate.
The oxidation-resistance improvement results from a stable, adherent barrier that limits oxygen diffusion at elevated temperatures.
A nickel-based superalloy can be susceptible to high-temperature oxidation.
ALD can be used to deposit an ultra-thin Al2O3 layer on a metallic substrate.
The proposed oxidation exposure is at elevated temperature in an oxidative atmosphere for an extended duration.
The intervention forms a continuous Al2O3 scale.
The intervention forms an adherent Al2O3 scale.
The intervention forms a pinhole-free Al2O3 scale.
The Al2O3 scale acts as a diffusion barrier.
The ALD-deposited Al2O3 layer has a dense microstructure that retards oxygen ingress.
Retarding oxygen ingress reduces the oxidation rate of the underlying metal.
The coated substrate will have a markedly thinner oxide scale than an uncoated substrate after oxidation testing.
The coated substrate will have markedly lower oxidation-related weight gain than an uncoated substrate.
An identical uncoated substrate tested under the same oxidation conditions provides the baseline.
Oxidation resistance improves only over the temperature range in which the Al2O3 coating remains stable and intact.
Extremely high temperatures or other conditions that compromise coating integrity can diminish the oxidation-resistance benefit.
The magnitude of oxidation-resistance improvement depends on coating uniformity.
The magnitude of oxidation-resistance improvement depends on coating adhesion quality.
The magnitude of oxidation-resistance improvement depends on the substrate alloy composition.
A lack of statistically significant reductions in both weight gain and oxide-scale thickness relative to an uncoated control would falsify the hypothesis.
